title: Sable and the Harvest
premise: Sable Joubert returns to her late grandmother's farmhouse to settle the estate alongside Gideon Joubert, a skeptical surveyor hired to appraise the property. But every photograph in the house now shows an extra chair at the kitchen table, and the house itself seems to appraise them back — measuring, weighing, deciding. Sable discovers her grandmother was the last keeper of a founding-family ritual that binds the land's hungry well, and when she is pulled bodily into the house's memory, she must finish what the founders started before the well refills on the harvest moon. In the end, Sable completes the ritual by offering not a life but the truth the founders buried — freeing the land, losing the house, and choosing love with Gideon over the duty her blood demands.
about_author: Orsen Lockridge is the pen name of a former rural land assessor who spent fifteen years cataloguing properties no one wanted to buy twice. He writes horror from a farmhouse he insists, in writing, has only four chairs.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Gideon Joubert arrives to survey the Joubert farmhouse for probate, meeting the wary granddaughter, Sable. His instruments give impossible readings — rooms larger inside than out. POV alternates between his dry professionalism and Sable's grief-numbed resentment of the house. Emotional beat: unease disguised as routine.

chapters.title: One Chair Too Many
chapters.summary: Sable sorts her grandmother's photographs and finds every family picture now includes an extra wooden chair at the table — including photos taken decades before the chair existed. Gideon dismisses it as double exposure. That night both hear a chair scrape across the empty kitchen floor. Beat: dread takes root.

chapters.title: What the Deed Doesn't Say
chapters.summary: In the county archive, Gideon finds the original 1847 deed naming a 'well covenant' among its covenants — an obligation to 'keep the water wanting.' The clerk who helps him goes pale and refuses to discuss the property further. Beat: the past has legal teeth.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Sable discovers her grandmother's hidden ledger: generations of Joubert women recording dates, offerings, and a countdown that ends this harvest moon. The final entry reads 'It will not be me. It will be the one who comes home.' Beat: inheritance revealed as sentence.

chapters.title: The Well Breathes
chapters.summary: Gideon measures the dry well and records a slow exhalation of warm air rising from it, timed like sleep-breathing. Sable dreams of descending it. They argue — she wants to leave, he insists on finishing the appraisal. Beat: denial begins to crack on both sides.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Look Away
chapters.summary: Sable visits the nearest farmstead; the family feeds her but won't cross their own threshold while she's there, and their children wear iron keys on cords. An old woman tells her only: 'Your grandmother kept it polite. Don't you let it get hungry.' Beat: isolation deepens.

chapters.title: Photographs Moving
chapters.summary: The extra chair in the photos has begun changing position night to night — closer to the camera each time. Sable realizes it is approaching whoever holds the photograph. She burns one; the smoke smells of her grandmother's kitchen. Beat: the haunting becomes personal targeting.

chapters.title: Gideon's Report
chapters.summary: Gideon drafts his appraisal and finds his typed pages rearranged overnight into a single repeated line: VALUED. He stays anyway — telling himself it's professional rigor, knowing it isn't. First admission of belief, spoken aloud to an empty room. Beat: skeptic bends.

chapters.title: The Founders' Chapel
chapters.summary: Following ledger clues, they find a collapsed chapel on the back acreage where five founder families sealed the covenant. Carved names include JOUBERT. One founder's name has been chiseled out. Beat: the family was complicit, not cursed by accident.

chapters.title: Sable Is Taken
chapters.summary: At dusk the kitchen fills with the smell of Sunday dinner, and Sable — answering a voice like her grandmother's — steps through the photograph's frame into the house's memory. Gideon watches her vanish mid-sentence. Beat: the blurb's promise lands; stakes become mortal.

chapters.title: Inside the House's Memory
chapters.summary: Sable walks the farmhouse as it stood in 1847, populated by founders who treat her as expected company. They seat her in the extra chair. She learns the ritual requires a keeper to remain — willingly or otherwise — before the well refills. Beat: captivity dressed as welcome.

chapters.title: The Chiseled Name
chapters.summary: In the memory, Sable finds the erased founder: a woman who refused the first offering and tried to end the covenant, erased from record and remembrance. Her ghost tends the well mouth, still keeping it 'wanting' against her will. Beat: hope — someone resisted.

chapters.title: Gideon Digs
chapters.summary: Alone, Gideon abandons the survey and excavates the chapel foundation, unearthing the founders' covenant stone with instructions half-legible: the ritual can be finished, not just fed. He speaks to the house itself, negotiating for Sable's return. Beat: loyalty over self-preservation.

chapters.title: Dinner With the Founders
chapters.summary: The memory-founders press Sable to accept the keeper's role, showing her loving visions of grandmother and home. Duty wears the face of family. She nearly says yes — then notices the vision's grandmother never meets her eyes. Beat: temptation at its most seductive.

chapters.title: The Refill Begins
chapters.summary: Water sounds rise from the real-world well; the town's dogs go silent; frost forms indoors despite October warmth. The erased woman's ghost tells Sable the truth the founders buried: the well was never owed anything — it was cheated, and the ritual is a lie of bookkeeping. Beat: theme crystallizes — power built on a false debt.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Gideon breaks through into the memory carrying the covenant stone, bleeding from the descent. He offers himself in Sable's place; she refuses to let him. Their argument becomes a confession of love conducted in front of the hungry founders. Beat: emotional climax of the relationship thread.

chapters.title: Reading the Stone
chapters.summary: Together they decipher the full covenant: the founders stole the water source from the erased woman's family and bound the land's grief with a ritual of substitution. Finishing the ritual 'as started' means completing the original crime. To free everyone, it must be finished differently — with truth instead of a body. Beat: the plan forms.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises
chapters.summary: The well begins refilling; the house convulses, walls breathing, photographs screaming light. The founders turn hostile as Sable carries the stone toward the well mouth, the erased woman walking beside her. Beat: race against the refill, tension at maximum.

chapters.title: Finishing the Ritual
chapters.summary: At the well, Sable speaks the founders' buried crime aloud — naming the erased woman, restoring her name to the stone — and offers acknowledgment instead of sacrifice. The well drinks the words. The founders dissolve mid-reach; the house exhales and goes still. Beat: climax resolved through truth, not power.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Water
chapters.summary: Morning: the well holds clear, cold water for the first time in living memory. The photographs show only the family, the extra chair gone — though one frame keeps a faint warmth where it stood. Sable grieves her grandmother properly at last. Beat: release and mourning.

chapters.title: The Appraisal Revised
chapters.summary: Gideon files a report valuing the house at exactly nothing, recommending demolition — his quiet act of loyalty to what happened there. Sable signs the estate papers, keeping only the ledger and the restored stone. Neighbors begin leaving bread on the porch, a thanks they don't explain. Beat: denouement, threads tied.

chapters.title: Sable and the Harvest
chapters.summary: A year later, Sable and Gideon plant the back acreage together. At harvest dinner, she sets the table — and pauses at a fifth chair, then leaves it standing open, neither feared nor filled. Some debts are honored by remembering, not repaying. Beat: peace earned, vigilance chosen, love settled into place.
